Total population; ages 40–90; years 1961–2005

1 Scope, data paths and the teaching script

This document completes Q3(a) and Q3(b). Its filename is retained as requested. It uses the lecturer’s StMoMo Poisson LC and Renshaw–Haberman (RH) methods. All estimates, tables, plotted values and numerical conclusions below are calculated when this document is knitted; no previous fitted objects or results are loaded.

Keep the four supplied TXT files in the data folder beside this Rmd. RStudio’s Knit command uses the Rmd folder as its default working directory. This document uses relative paths, not file.choose() or a guessed desktop path. If needed, edit params: data_dir: above to the actual data folder. Missing files cause an explicit error before any model is fitted.

The teaching example uses Male, ages 20–89 and years 1981–2021. These are changed to Total, ages 40–90 and years 1961–2005. Forecasting blocks and age-50 forecast comparisons are omitted because Q3 does not request them. The original script’s late references to the undefined RH.simple.fit would cause errors: the Q3(b) implementation below consistently uses the actual object RH.fit. RH-related code is retained only for part (b), not for the LC analysis in part (a).

1.1 Read and verify the original text files

files <- data.frame(
  country=c("AUS", "AUS", "UK", "UK"),
  kind=c("Deaths", "Exposures", "Deaths", "Exposures"),
  filename=c("AUS_Deaths_1x1.txt", "AUS_Exposures_1x1.txt",
             "UK_Deaths_1x1.txt", "UK_Exposures_1x1.txt"),
  stringsAsFactors=FALSE
)
files$path <- file.path(data_dir, files$filename)
if (any(!file.exists(files$path))) {
  stop("Missing data files: ", paste(files$path[!file.exists(files$path)], collapse=", "),
       ". Keep the data folder beside this Rmd; current directory is ", getwd())
}

read_hmd <- function(path, country, kind) {
  first_lines <- readLines(path, n=10, warn=FALSE)
  expected_country <- unname(country_names[country])
  if (!startsWith(first_lines[1], paste0(expected_country, ",")))
    stop("Country mismatch in ", path, ": ", first_lines[1])
  expected_kind <- if (kind=="Deaths") "Deaths" else "Exposure"
  if (!grepl(expected_kind, first_lines[1], fixed=TRUE))
    stop("Deaths/exposures file mismatch: ", path)
  header_row <- grep("^\\s*Year\\s+Age\\s+", first_lines)
  if (length(header_row)!=1L) stop("Cannot locate unique Year/Age header: ", path)
  # For all four inspected files header_row=3, hence skip=2.
  # Detecting it also protects against different numbers of description lines.
  raw <- read.table(path, skip=header_row-1L, header=TRUE,
                    stringsAsFactors=FALSE, na.strings=".")
  required_columns <- c("Year", "Age", "Female", "Male", "Total")
  if (!all(required_columns %in% names(raw)))
    stop("Unexpected file columns in ", path)
  raw$Age_num <- as.numeric(gsub("\\+", "", as.character(raw$Age)))
  list(raw=raw, header=first_lines[1], skipped=header_row-1L)
}

loaded <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(files)), function(i)
  read_hmd(files$path[i], files$country[i], files$kind[i]))
files$description <- vapply(loaded, `[[`, character(1), "header")
files$lines_skipped <- vapply(loaded, `[[`, integer(1), "skipped")
knitr::kable(files[c("filename", "lines_skipped", "description")],
             caption="Actual filenames and country/type checks from the file headers")

1.2 Construct age-by-year matrices and check the data

make_population <- function(country) {
  death_i <- which(files$country==country & files$kind=="Deaths")
  exposure_i <- which(files$country==country & files$kind=="Exposures")
  d <- loaded[[death_i]]$raw
  e <- loaded[[exposure_i]]$raw
  d <- subset(d, Year %in% years.fit & Age_num %in% ages.fit)
  e <- subset(e, Year %in% years.fit & Age_num %in% ages.fit)
  expected_n <- length(ages.fit)*length(years.fit)
  if (nrow(d)!=expected_n || nrow(e)!=expected_n ||
      anyDuplicated(d[c("Age_num", "Year")]) ||
      anyDuplicated(e[c("Age_num", "Year")]))
    stop("Incomplete or duplicate age/year grid for ", country)
  # IMPORTANT: Total (both sexes); rows=age and columns=calendar year.
  Dxt <- acast(d, Age_num ~ Year, value.var="Total")
  Ext <- acast(e, Age_num ~ Year, value.var="Total")
  Dxt <- as.matrix(Dxt[as.character(ages.fit), as.character(years.fit)])
  Ext <- as.matrix(Ext[as.character(ages.fit), as.character(years.fit)])
  stopifnot(identical(dim(Dxt), c(51L,45L)), identical(dim(Ext), c(51L,45L)),
            identical(rownames(Dxt), as.character(ages.fit)),
            identical(colnames(Dxt), as.character(years.fit)),
            identical(dimnames(Dxt), dimnames(Ext)))
  if (any(!is.finite(Dxt)) || any(!is.finite(Ext)) ||
      any(Dxt<0) || any(Ext<=0)) stop("Invalid selected data: ", country)
  list(Dxt=Dxt, Ext=Ext)
}
populations <- lapply(names(country_names), make_population)
names(populations) <- names(country_names)

checks <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(populations), function(country) {
  z <- populations[[country]]
  data.frame(Country=country_names[country],
    Dxt_rows=nrow(z$Dxt), Dxt_columns=ncol(z$Dxt),
    Ext_rows=nrow(z$Ext), Ext_columns=ncol(z$Ext),
    Age_range=paste(range(as.integer(rownames(z$Dxt))),collapse="–"),
    Year_range=paste(range(as.integer(colnames(z$Dxt))),collapse="–"),
    Missing_D=sum(is.na(z$Dxt)), Missing_E=sum(is.na(z$Ext)),
    Negative_D=sum(z$Dxt<0), Nonpositive_E=sum(z$Ext<=0),
    Zero_D=sum(z$Dxt==0),
    Nonfinite_log_rates=sum(!is.finite(log(z$Dxt/z$Ext))),row.names=NULL)
}))
knitr::kable(checks, caption="Checks on the selected 51-by-45 grids")

Australia 51 45 51 45 40–90 1961–2005 0 0 0 0 0 0

stopifnot(all(checks$Nonfinite_log_rates==0))

Each matrix has 51 age rows and 45 year columns, or 2295 cells. The table reports missing and invalid observations explicitly. No ages or years are silently dropped, no missing rates are imputed, and the provided HMD death values are not rounded.

2 Q3(a): Lee–Carter models

For each population the model is \[ D_{x,t}\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(E^c_{x,t}m_{x,t}),\qquad \log m_{x,t}=a_x+b_xk_t. \] Here \(a_x\) describes the baseline age pattern of log mortality; \(k_t\) is the common period index; and \(b_x\) measures the sensitivity of log mortality at age \(x\) to changes in that index. The usual LC constraints \(\sum_xb_x=1\) and \(\sum_tk_t=0\) identify the scale and location. Deaths and exposures are supplied directly to StMoMo::fit, following the teacher’s example.

LC <- lc(link="log")
LC.fits <- lapply(populations, function(z)
  fit(LC, Dxt=z$Dxt, Ext=z$Ext, ages=ages.fit, years=years.fit, verbose=FALSE))
if (!all(vapply(LC.fits, function(f) isTRUE(f$conv), logical(1))))
  stop("At least one LC model did not converge; do not interpret it as a completed fit.")
fit_checks <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(LC.fits), function(country) {
  f <- LC.fits[[country]]
  data.frame(Country=country_names[country], Converged=f$conv,
             Cells=f$nobs, Parameters=f$npar, Poisson_deviance=f$deviance,
             Sum_bx=sum(f$bx[,1]), Sum_kt=sum(f$kt),row.names=NULL)
}))
knitr::kable(fit_checks, digits=6,caption="LC fitting results calculated during Knit")
LC fitting results calculated during Knit
Country Converged Cells Parameters Poisson_deviance Sum_bx Sum_kt
Australia TRUE 2295 145 5993.579 1 0
United Kingdom TRUE 2295 145 25591.761 1 0

2.1 Estimated parameters

par(mfrow=c(2,3), mar=c(4,4,3,1))
for (country in names(LC.fits)) {
  f <- LC.fits[[country]]
  label <- country_names[country]
  plot(ages.fit, f$ax, type="l", col="#17365D", xlab="Age x", ylab=expression(a[x]),
       main=paste(label, "LC: age effect"),
       ylim=range(unlist(lapply(LC.fits, `[[`, "ax"))))
  plot(ages.fit, f$bx[,1], type="l", col="#17365D", xlab="Age x", ylab=expression(b[x]),
       main=paste(label, "LC: age sensitivity"),
       ylim=range(unlist(lapply(LC.fits, `[[`, "bx"))))
  plot(years.fit, f$kt[1,], type="l", col="#17365D", xlab="Calendar year t", ylab=expression(k[t]),
       main=paste(label, "LC: period index"),
       ylim=range(unlist(lapply(LC.fits, `[[`, "kt"))))
}

Estimated LC parameters. Common axis limits are used within each parameter column.

Australia. The estimated age effect rises from -6.393 at age 40 to -1.625 at age 90, consistent with higher mortality at older ages. The largest estimated age sensitivity occurs at age 54. The period index changes from 15.70 in 1961 to -28.52 in 2005.

United Kingdom. The estimated age effect rises from -6.408 at age 40 to -1.547 at age 90, consistent with higher mortality at older ages. The largest estimated age sensitivity occurs at age 58. The period index changes from 13.64 in 1961 to -21.23 in 2005.

Both countries have positive age sensitivities and an overall decline in the period index, indicating broad mortality improvement. The plots show fluctuations rather than an exactly monotone trend. The sensitivity curves peak in middle age and are lower at the oldest ages. Parameter magnitudes are model-specific; a cross-country difference in k_t is not itself a mortality-rate difference.

2.2 Age–year residual maps and cohort evidence

The unscaled Poisson deviance residual is \[ r_{x,t}=\operatorname{sign}(D_{x,t}-\hat D_{x,t}) \sqrt{2\left[D_{x,t}\log\left(\frac{D_{x,t}}{\hat D_{x,t}}\right) -(D_{x,t}-\hat D_{x,t})\right]},\qquad \hat D_{x,t}=E^c_{x,t}\hat m_{x,t}. \] We use residuals(fit, scale=FALSE) and common symmetric colour limits. StMoMo internally adds 0.00001 to deaths when calculating its residuals to handle possible zeros; the input data used for fitting remain unchanged.

Red denotes observed deaths above the fitted level; blue denotes deaths below it. Both magnitude and sign appear on the colour scale. With calendar year horizontal and age vertical, observations with a common birth year \(c=t-x\) follow an upward-sloping diagonal, \(x=t-c\). Persistent same-sign bands along these paths suggest an omitted cohort effect: LC has only an age profile and a common period factor, with no separate term for year of birth.

LC.res <- lapply(LC.fits, function(f) residuals(f,scale=FALSE)$residuals)

cohort_guides <- function() {
  for (c in seq(1880,1960,20)) {
    age <- years.fit-c
    ok <- age>=min(ages.fit) & age<=max(ages.fit)
    lines(years.fit[ok], age[ok], col="#555555", lty=3, lwd=.6)
  }
}
plot_residual_pair <- function(mats, titles) {
  limit <- max(abs(unlist(mats)),na.rm=TRUE)
  colours <- colorRampPalette(c("#2166AC","white","#B2182B"))(101)
  par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(4,4,3,6))
  for (i in seq_along(mats)) {
    fields::image.plot(years.fit, ages.fit, t(mats[[i]]),
      zlim=c(-limit,limit), col=colours, useRaster=TRUE,
      xlab="Calendar year t", ylab="Age x", main=titles[i],
      legend.lab="", legend.cex=.8, legend.mar=4)
    cohort_guides(); box()
  }
}
plot_residual_pair(LC.res,paste(country_names[names(LC.res)],"LC residuals"))

LC residuals for both countries, using matching scales. Dotted guides follow constant birth cohorts.

Because larger populations can have larger residual magnitudes, the following sign-only maps provide an additional check on the coherence of the diagonal patterns, rather than identifying the country solely from residual size.

plot_sign_pair <- function(mats,titles) {
  par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(4,4,3,1),oma=c(2,0,0,0))
  for(i in seq_along(mats)) {
    image(years.fit,ages.fit,t(sign(mats[[i]])),
          breaks=c(-1.5,-.5,.5,1.5),col=c("#2166AC","white","#B2182B"),
          xlab="Calendar year t",ylab="Age x",main=titles[i],useRaster=TRUE)
    cohort_guides();box()
  }
  mtext("Blue = negative; white = zero; red = positive. Dotted guides = constant birth cohorts.",
        side=1,outer=TRUE,cex=.8)
}
plot_sign_pair(LC.res,paste(country_names[names(LC.res)],"LC residual signs"))

Signs of LC residuals. Blue: observed below fitted; red: observed above fitted; white: zero.

2.2.1 Data-driven comparison of the diagonal patterns

To make the choice for part (b) reproducible rather than hard-coding a country, we also summarise the sign coherence along each actual cohort diagonal. Let \(s_{x,t}=\operatorname{sign}(r_{x,t})\) and let \(\bar s_c\) be its mean on cohort \(c\). The descriptive score is \[ C=\frac{1}{N}\sum_c n_c\bar s_c^2. \] It is larger when residual signs agree more strongly along cohorts. All fitted cells are retained, and both populations have the same grid. This is not a hypothesis test, a new fitting objective or proof of causality; the residual maps remain the principal visual evidence. Unlike total deviance, this summary does not automatically increase with the magnitude of exposure.

cohort_sign_score <- function(mat) {
  cohort <- as.vector(outer(ages.fit,years.fit,function(x,t)t-x))
  groups <- split(as.vector(sign(mat)),cohort)
  n <- lengths(groups)
  means <- vapply(groups,mean,numeric(1))
  sum(n*means^2)/sum(n)
}
scores <- vapply(LC.res,cohort_sign_score,numeric(1))
if (abs(diff(scores))<1e-8) stop("Cohort sign scores tie; inspect the maps before selecting part (b).")
selected_country <- names(which.max(scores))
selected_name <- unname(country_names[selected_country])
other_country <- setdiff(names(scores),selected_country)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Country=country_names[names(scores)],
                       Cohort_sign_coherence=as.numeric(scores)),digits=4,
             caption="Descriptive sign coherence along birth-cohort diagonals")
Descriptive sign coherence along birth-cohort diagonals
Country Cohort_sign_coherence
AUS Australia 0.2678
UK United Kingdom 0.4721

For these supplied data, United Kingdom has the higher diagonal sign-coherence score (0.4721 versus 0.2678 for Australia). The generated maps show more persistent same-sign diagonal bands in this population, whereas the other population’s pattern is more fragmented. The evidence therefore points to United Kingdom as having the stronger omitted cohort structure. This does not imply that cohort structure is completely absent in the other population, or that every diagonal feature has a known causal explanation.

3 Q3(b): Adding a cohort effect

For the population identified above, we retain the teacher’s Renshaw–Haberman model: \[ \log m_{x,t}=a_x+b_xk_t+c_xh_{t-x}. \] Here \(h_{t-x}\) is the birth-cohort factor and \(c_x\) its age sensitivity. This is the age-modulated cohort extension in the supplied R example, not an unrelated APC model. The same deaths, exposures and full fitting window are used. approxConst=TRUE and the package’s identifiability constraints follow the teacher’s implementation. No forecasts are needed for this question.

RH <- rh(link="log",cohortAgeFun="NP",approxConst=TRUE)
z <- populations[[selected_country]]
RH.fit <- fit(RH,Dxt=z$Dxt,Ext=z$Ext,ages=ages.fit,years=years.fit,verbose=FALSE)
if (!isTRUE(RH.fit$conv)) stop("RH did not converge: do not report its fit as completed.")
RH.res <- residuals(RH.fit,scale=FALSE)$residuals
stopifnot(identical(dim(RH.res),dim(LC.res[[selected_country]])))
plot_residual_pair(list(LC.res[[selected_country]],RH.res),
                   paste(selected_name,c("LC residuals","RH residuals")))

Before and after adding the cohort term: identical residual definition, age/year axes and colour limits. 

plot_sign_pair(list(LC.res[[selected_country]],RH.res),
               paste(selected_name,c("LC residual signs","RH residual signs")))

Residual signs for the selected population before and after the RH cohort term. 

chosen_LC <- LC.fits[[selected_country]]
comparison <- data.frame(Model=c("LC","RH"),
  Converged=c(chosen_LC$conv,RH.fit$conv),
  Cells=c(chosen_LC$nobs,RH.fit$nobs),
  Parameters=c(chosen_LC$npar,RH.fit$npar),
  Poisson_deviance=c(chosen_LC$deviance,RH.fit$deviance),
  Log_rate_RMSE=c(
    sqrt(mean((log(z$Dxt/z$Ext)-log(fitted(chosen_LC,type="rates")))^2)),
    sqrt(mean((log(z$Dxt/z$Ext)-log(fitted(RH.fit,type="rates")))^2))),
  Cohort_sign_coherence=c(scores[selected_country],cohort_sign_score(RH.res)))
knitr::kable(comparison,digits=6,caption=paste(selected_name,"LC/RH diagnostics"))
United Kingdom LC/RH diagnostics
Model Converged Cells Parameters Poisson_deviance Log_rate_RMSE Cohort_sign_coherence
UK LC TRUE 2295 145 25591.761 0.042000 0.472085
RH TRUE 2295 288 4278.376 0.017727 0.023733 
reduction <- 100*(1-RH.fit$deviance/chosen_LC$deviance)
coherence_reduced <- cohort_sign_score(RH.res)<scores[selected_country]

The United Kingdom Poisson deviance changes from 25,591.761 under LC to 4,278.376 under RH, a reduction of 83.3%. The cohort sign-coherence score also decreases. For the supplied data, the before/after maps show weaker, less persistent same-sign cohort strips and a more mixed residual pattern after including the cohort term.

RH can improve this feature because people born in the same year share the factor \(h_{t-x}\) across different ages and calendar years. LC’s single period factor does not explicitly allow this birth-year structure. The extra term addresses the specific diagonal pattern identified in part (a). Nevertheless, residual structure is not necessarily eliminated. RH has more parameters, so the deviance reduction is descriptive in-sample evidence, not a formal chi-square likelihood-ratio test or a claim of superior future forecasts. Cohorts at the boundaries have fewer observations and their parameters should be interpreted cautiously.
